<problem>
Let \(\mathcal Q\) be the set of odd prime powers. For \(q\in\mathcal Q\), put \(V=\mathbb F_q^4\) and \(m=(q^2+1)/2\). Choose collections \(\mathcal S_1,\ldots,\mathcal S_m\) of two-dimensional linear subspaces of \(V\) satisfying:

- For each \(i\), the sets \(D\setminus\{0\}\), with \(D\in\mathcal S_i\), partition \(V\setminus\{0\}\).
- No two-dimensional subspace belongs to two different collections \(\mathcal S_i\).

Such collections exist for every \(q\in\mathcal Q\). You may use that the polynomial defined below is independent of their choice.

Let \(X=\{p_1,\ldots,p_m\}\) be disjoint from \(V\), and set \(E=V\sqcup X\). Define a ranked poset \(\mathcal L_q\), ordered by inclusion, whose elements are the following subsets of \(E\):

- Rank \(0\): \(\varnothing\).
- Rank \(1\): all singletons.
- Rank \(2\): all affine lines in \(V\), and all two-element subsets of \(E\) meeting \(X\).
- Rank \(3\): all affine planes \(a+D\) with \(D\notin\bigcup_i\mathcal S_i\); all sets \((a+D)\cup\{p_i\}\) with \(D\in\mathcal S_i\); and all three-element subsets of \(E\) containing at least two elements of \(X\).
- Rank \(4\): \(E\).

Here an affine line or plane is a translate of a one- or two-dimensional linear subspace, respectively, and repeated descriptions of the same subset give only one poset element.

Form \(\mathcal K_q\) by retaining from \(\mathcal L_q\times\mathcal L_q\times\{0<1\}\) all triples \((F_1,F_2,b)\) with
\[
\operatorname{rk}(F_1)+\operatorname{rk}(F_2)+b\leq 6,
\]
ordered coordinatewise and ranked by this sum, and then adjoining one new maximum element of rank \(7\).

For \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,6\}\), let \(\alpha_q(S)\) be the number of strict chains in \(\mathcal K_q\) whose set of ranks is exactly \(S\), with \(\alpha_q(\varnothing)=1\), and define
\[
\beta_q(S)=\sum_{T\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S|-|T|}\alpha_q(T).
\]
A set of integers is called stable if it contains no two consecutive integers. Define
\[
H_q(t)=\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq\{2,3,4,5,6\}\\S\text{ stable}}}
\beta_q(S)t^{|S|}(1+t)^{6-2|S|}
=\sum_{i=0}^{6}a_i(q)t^i.
\]
This normalization gives the Chow polynomial of the rank-seven matroid with lattice of flats \(\mathcal K_q\).

Determine the exact ordered pair \((\mathcal R,\mathcal C)\), where
\[
\mathcal R=\{q\in\mathcal Q:H_q(t)\text{ has a nonreal zero}\},
\qquad
\mathcal C=\{q\in\mathcal Q:a_i(q)^2<a_{i-1}(q)a_{i+1}(q)\text{ for some }1\leq i\leq5\}.
\]
Describe both sets by explicit conditions on \(q\).
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer is an exact ordered pair (𝓡, 𝓒), with each set described by an explicit condition on q that decides membership for every odd prime power q: whether H_q has a nonreal zero, and whether its coefficient sequence has a strict log-concavity violation, respectively.

12	## 1. Flag counts in \(\mathcal L_q\)
13	
14	Write
15	\[
16	m=\frac{q^2+1}{2},\qquad N=q^4+m.
17	\]
18	The number of affine lines in \(V\), and the number of rank-two flats meeting \(X\), respectively, are
19	\[
20	L=q^3(q^3+q^2+q+1),\qquad
21	B=mq^4+\binom m2.
22	\]
23	
24	There are
25	\[
26	G=(q^2+1)(q^2+q+1)
27	\]
28	two-dimensional linear subspaces of \(V\). Each \(\mathcal S_i\) has \(q^2+1\) members, since its nonzero vectors partition \(V\setminus\{0\}\). Consequently, the counts of the three types of rank-three flats are
29	\[
30	\begin{aligned}
31	P&=q^2\bigl(G-m(q^2+1)\bigr),\\
32	A&=q^2m(q^2+1),\\
33	T&=\binom m2q^4+\binom m3.

36	Their internal incidences are as follows:
37	\[
38	\begin{array}{c|r|r|r}
39	\text{number of flats}&\text{points per flat}&
40	q\text{-point rank-two flats}&2\text{-point rank-two flats}\\ \hline
41	P&q^2&q(q+1)&0\\
42	A&q^2+1&q(q+1)&q^2\\
43	T&3&0&3
44	\end{array}
45	\]
46	For example, an augmented plane has all the affine lines of its underlying plane and the \(q^2\) pairs joining its distinguished point \(p_i\) to the plane.
47	
48	For \(J\subseteq\{1,2,3\}\), let \(f_J\) be the number of chains of \(\mathcal L_q\) with rank set \(J\). Then
49	\[
50	\begin{array}{c|l}
51	J&f_J\\ \hline
52	\varnothing&1\\
53	1&N\\
54	2&L+B\\
55	3&P+A+T\\
56	12&qL+2B\\
57	13&Pq^2+A(q^2+1)+3T\\
58	23&Pq(q+1)+A\bigl(q(q+1)+q^2\bigr)+3T\\
59	123&Pq^2(q+1)+A(q^3+3q^2)+6T.
60	\end{array}                                                    \tag{1}
61	\]
62	Ranks zero and four may be added to a chain without changing its count, because each has a unique element.
63	
64	These formulas also show directly why the calculation is independent of the chosen collections.
65	
66	## 2. Computing the three gamma coefficients
67	
68	Define \(g_1,g_2,g_3\) by
69	\[
70	H_q(t)=(1+t)^6+g_1t(1+t)^4+g_2t^2(1+t)^2+g_3t^3.       \tag{2}
71	\]
72	
73	Here is an exact rule for obtaining them from (1). If
74	\(S=\{s_1<\cdots<s_k\}\subseteq\{2,\ldots,6\}\), then
75	\[
76	\alpha_q(S)=
77	\sum_{\substack{
78	0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_k\le4\\
79	0\le u_1\le\cdots\le u_k\le4\\
80	0\le b_1\le\cdots\le b_k\le1\\
81	r_j+u_j+b_j=s_j}}
82	f_{\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}\cap\{1,2,3\}}\,
83	f_{\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}\cap\{1,2,3\}}.                     \tag{3}
84	\]
85	Indeed, the ranks in each product coordinate are weakly increasing. Once these rank sequences are fixed, the two factors in (3) count the possible coordinate chains; the \(\{0<1\}\) coordinate has exactly one choice.
86	
87	All ranks in question are at most six, so the truncation and the newly adjoined maximum do not change these counts. Applying the stated inclusion-exclusion formula to (3) gives the required \(\beta_q(S)\), and summing over stable sets of size \(j\) gives \(g_j\).
88

90	\[
91	u=f_1,\quad v=f_2,\quad w=f_3,\quad x=f_{12},
92	\quad r=f_{13}+f_{23},\quad h=f_{123}.
93	\]
94	In particular,
95	\[
96	r=P(2q^2+q)+A(3q^2+q+1)+6T.
97	\]

99	\[
100	\begin{aligned}
101	g_1={}&2u^2+4uv+4uw+6u+2v^2+4vw+6v+w^2+4w-1,\\
102	g_2={}&3u^2+10uv+4uw-10u+6v^2+4vw-6v-w^2-6w-2\\
103	&+6x(u+v+w)+8r(u+v)+2wr+3x^2+6xr+r^2+2r,\\
104	g_3={}&h^2+6hx-3u^2-2uw-2ux+2ur+v^2-2vw+2vr-2v\\
105	&+w^2-6wx-2wr+2w+x^2+6xr+r^2-2r+1.
106	\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
107	\]
108	The program below verifies (4) against (3), rather than assuming these formulas.

110	Expanding (2), we obtain
111	\[
112	\begin{aligned}
113	a_0=a_6&=1,\\
114	a_1=a_5&=6+g_1,\\
115	a_2=a_4&=15+4g_1+g_2,\\

117	\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{5}
118	\]

120	## 3. Exact sign certificates
121	
122	Set
123	\[
124	F_q(z)=z^3+g_1z^2+g_2z+g_3,\qquad
125	D(q)=\operatorname{disc}_z(F_q),
126	\]
127	and
128	\[
129	C_1(q)=a_1^2-a_0a_2,\qquad
130	C_2(q)=a_2^2-a_1a_3.
131	\]
132	
133	The following table gives the signs of **every coefficient** after shifting \(q=3+s\). Thus, for example, the row for \(D\) says that the coefficients of \(s^0,\ldots,s^{60}\) are positive and those of \(s^{61},\ldots,s^{66}\) are negative. There are no zero coefficients in the table.
134	\[
135	\begin{array}{c|r|l}
136	\text{polynomial}&\text{degree}&
137	\text{coefficient signs after }q=3+s\\ \hline
138	g_1&16&+\text{ for }0\le j\le16\\
139	g_2&16&+\text{ for }0\le j\le16\\
140	g_3&18&+\text{ for }0\le j\le18\\
141	C_1&32&+\text{ for }0\le j\le32\\
142	D&66&+\text{ for }0\le j\le60,\quad-\text{ for }61\le j\le66\\
143	C_2&34&+\text{ for }0\le j\le32,\quad-\text{ for }33\le j\le34
144	\end{array}                                                       \tag{6}
145	\]
146	The endpoint signs are
147	\[
148	D(44)>0,\qquad D(45)<0,\qquad
149	C_2(90)>0,\qquad C_2(91)<0.                              \tag{7}
150	\]
151	All statements in (6)–(7) are checked using exact rational arithmetic by the supplied program.
152	
153	In particular,
154	\[
155	g_1,g_2,g_3,C_1>0\qquad(q\ge3).                           \tag{8}
156	\]
157	By Descartes’ rule of signs, each of \(D(3+s)\) and \(C_2(3+s)\) has exactly one positive real zero: its coefficient sequence has exactly one sign change, and (7) also supplies a positive zero. Thus
158	\[
159	\begin{array}{c|cc}
160	&\text{positive}&\text{negative}\\ \hline
161	D(q),\quad q\in\mathbb Z,\ q\ge3&q\le44&q\ge45\\
162	C_2(q),\quad q\in\mathbb Z,\ q\ge3&q\le90&q\ge91.
163	\end{array}                                                       \tag{9}
164	\]
165	Neither polynomial vanishes at an integer \(q\ge3\).
166	
167	## 4. Nonreal zeros
168	
169	From (2),
170	\[
171	H_q(t)=t^3F_q\!\left(\frac{(1+t)^2}{t}\right).             \tag{10}
172	\]
173	Because all three \(g_j\) are positive, \(F_q\) has no nonnegative real zero.
174	
175	If \(D(q)>0\), the cubic has three distinct real zeros, all negative. For each such zero \(z\), the corresponding quadratic factor of \(H_q\) is
176	\[
177	t^2+(2-z)t+1.
178	\]
179	Since \(z<0\), this quadratic has two real negative zeros. Hence \(H_q\) is real-rooted.
180	
181	If \(D(q)<0\), the cubic has nonreal zeros. A nonreal value of \(z\) cannot equal \((1+t)^2/t\) for real nonzero \(t\), so (10) implies that \(H_q\) has nonreal zeros.
182	
183	It follows from (9) that, for integer \(q\ge3\),
184	\[
185	H_q\text{ has a nonreal zero}\iff q\ge45.
186	\]
187	The integer \(45=3^2\cdot5\) is not a prime power, so on \(\mathcal Q\) this is exactly \(q\ge47\). Therefore
188	\[
189	\mathcal R=\{q\in\mathcal Q:q\ge47\}.
190	\]
191	
192	## 5. Failure of log-concavity
193	
194	By symmetry in (5), there are only three distinct log-concavity differences:
195	\[
196	C_1,\qquad C_2,\qquad C_3=a_3^2-a_2^2.
197	\]
198	We already know \(C_1>0\). Moreover,
199	\[
200	a_3-a_2=5+2g_1+g_2+g_3>0,
201	\]
202	and \(a_3+a_2>0\), so \(C_3>0\). Consequently, failure of log-concavity occurs exactly when \(C_2<0\).
203	
204	By (9), this is equivalent to \(q\ge91\). None of
205	\[
206	91=7\cdot13,\qquad93=3\cdot31,\qquad95=5\cdot19
207	\]
208	is a prime power. Hence, among odd prime powers, the condition is exactly \(q\ge97\). Thus
209	\[
210	\mathcal C=\{q\in\mathcal Q:q\ge97\}.
211	\]
212	
213	## 6. Reproducible exact Python verification
214
